intro: Taiwan is an island off the coast of China, home to Indigenous peoples for thousands of years. It has been governed separately from mainland China since 1949, and its status is one of the world's most sensitive questions.

chapters.title: Indigenous Taiwan
text: Austronesian peoples have lived on Taiwan for at least 6,000 years. Many linguists think the Austronesian languages, now spoken from Madagascar to Hawaii, spread out from Taiwan.
Today 16 Indigenous peoples are officially recognised.

chapters.title: Dutch, Qing and Japanese rule
text: The Dutch set up a base in the south in 1624. In 1662 Koxinga, a Ming loyalist, drove them out. The Qing dynasty took over in 1683, and many settlers came from Fujian and Guangdong.
After China lost a war in 1895, Japan ruled Taiwan for 50 years, building railways and schools.

chapters.title: The Republic of China on Taiwan
text: After World War Two the Republic of China took over Taiwan. In the 1947 'February 28 Incident' thousands were killed in a crackdown. In 1949 the ROC government, led by Chiang Kai-shek's Kuomintang (KMT), lost the civil war to the Communists and retreated to Taiwan.
Martial law lasted until 1987. Taiwan then became a democracy, holding its first direct presidential election in 1996.

highlight.title: Two governments
highlight.text: Since 1949, the People's Republic of China has governed the mainland and the Republic of China has governed Taiwan.

chapters.title: A disputed status
text: The People's Republic of China claims Taiwan as part of its territory and has not ruled out force. Most countries do not formally recognise Taiwan as a separate country but keep close unofficial ties with it. Most people in Taiwan prefer to keep the current situation.

timeline.title: Qing rule
timeline.text: Taiwan becomes part of the Qing empire.

keyTerms.meaning: A family of languages and peoples across the Pacific and Indian Oceans.
